PCB opens direct signings window for PSL teams, announces pre-season roadmap. The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Friday opened the direct signings window for all eight HBL Pakistan Super League (PSL) franchises and unveiled the pre-season roadmap for the 12th edition of the tournament, which will be held from March 18 to May 2 next year. The player-movement cycle has begun with immediate effect, with the Player Auction scheduled for Jan 23 next year. HBL PSL 12 will feature 44 matches, comprising 40 league fixtures and four playoffs, over 46 days. For the first time in the league’s history, matches will be played across five to six venues. Under the direct signings rules, each franchise will be allowed to sign one marquee player who did not feature in either HBL PSL 10 or HBL PSL 11. The window will remain open until Nov 23. A workshop involving the franchises next week will finalise retention deadlines, the pre-auction trade window, auction regulations and playing conditions. In a significant development for domestic cricket, the PCB has formally aligned the National T20 Gold and National T20 Silver tournaments with the PSL pre-season calendar. The two competitions will now serve as the primary talent-identification pathway, providing outstanding domestic performers with a clearer route into the franchise league and potentially earning them selection for the national team. PCB Chairman Mohsin Naqvi described the upcoming season as the league’s most ambitious edition yet. “HBL PSL is Pakistan cricket’s biggest stage, and Season 12 will be its most ambitious yet. HBL PSL 11 ended before a record crowd, and we are building on that momentum by taking the league to more cities than ever before,” he said in a statement. “The roadmap we have finalised and are partially announcing today gives every stakeholder, from franchises and players to commercial partners and broadcasters, the certainty to plan at the highest level. With the foundations now in place, we are looking forward to an exciting season.” HBL PSL Chief Executive Officer Salman Naseer also highlighted the league’s expanded geographical reach, saying the move to multiple venues would bring the competition closer to fans across the country. “For the first time, HBL PSL will go to five to six venues, bringing the league closer to fans across Pakistan and giving more cities the chance to host the best of T20 cricket,” he said. “From today, the race to build the best squad for HBL PSL 12 is on. Every Direct Signing, every trade, every retention decision over the coming weeks will shape the teams that take the field in March. We look forward to a season that takes this league further than it has ever gone.” The announcement builds on the landmark 2026 season, when the PSL expanded to eight teams with the inclusion of Hyderabad Kingsmen and Rawalpindiz. Peshawar Zalmi claimed their second title after defeating debutants Hyderabad Kingsmen in the final at Gaddafi Stadium, which drew a record crowd of 32,461. The season, however, was also affected by regional tensions and fuel shortages, forcing organisers to concentrate most of the matches in Lahore and Karachi. Further details regarding venues, the complete schedule and commercial arrangements are expected to be announced in the coming weeks as franchises begin assembling their squads for the tournament. The PCB hopes the next edition will deliver a broader and more accessible experience for fans of Pakistan’s premier T20 competition.

Taiwan shuts down ahead of Typhoon Champi, nearly 1,000 flights cancelled. Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, and though the storm is weakening it could still make direct landfall on the island. At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of around 191 kph near its centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA). The storm was about 220 km east of Taiwan, the CWA said. The storm’s forecast track shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan. One person was killed and 171 were injured in Taiwan, where the government said 2,639 people had been evacuated from mountainous areas. Taipower said more than 77,000 homes had lost power, though electricity had already been restored to most. Typhoon Champi swirls over the Philippine Sea, as seen from space on October 23, 2026 in this screengrab taken from a handout GIF image. —CSU/CIRA and JMA/JAXA/Handout via Reuters CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng told Reuters that landfall could not be ruled out if it “stalls, loops, or wobbles from side to side” on approach to Taiwan. “The storm’s wind radius is quite large, among the bigger ones in recent years,” Liu said. “If the storm slows down, the strong winds will affect Taiwan for longer.” Coastal towns received mobile phone alerts warning of gusts exceeding 150 kph and urging residents to seek immediate shelter, while nearly a metre of rain was forecast for northern mountain areas, including around Taipei. In the northeastern county of Yilan, where strong winds and heavy showers were intensifying and the typhoon was forecast to pass close by later on Friday, authorities distributed sandbags and put amphibious vehicles and inflatable rescue boats on standby. A pedestrian holds an umbrella in strong winds as Typhoon Champi approaches Taiwan, in Keelung, Taiwan on October 23, 2026. —Reuters “When necessary, the military will come in to help people, including using amphibious vehicles for evacuations or disaster relief,” said Lee Ming-chen, head of the port town of Suao, which was badly flooded in previous typhoons. In the northern port city of Keelung, boat owners hurried to secure their vessels. “It’s not that severe; I’m just worried that there will be flooding. Keelung has seen a lot of flooding this year,” said construction worker Liu Yu-en, 18. Huge radius Taiwan forecasters said the storm’s radius was around 320 km, large enough to cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two days. Taiwan’s financial markets also closed on Friday, while only the Taiwan-controlled Kinmen islands, which sit next to the Chinese coast, will open schools and offices as normal. A fisherman walks among fishing nets at a fishing port as Typhoon Champi approaches Taiwan, in Keelung, Taiwan on October 23, 2026. —Reuters The transport ministry said all 262 domestic flights were cancelled for Friday, along with 717 international ones. The north-south high-speed rail service was operating as usual. In the capital Taipei there were squally showers, but public transport including the subway was working, albeit with reduced service. Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike in autumn too. The typhoon is forecast to first pass over Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, Yonaguni, in Okinawa Prefecture.

Lahore tops global pollution ranking as air quality turns ‘hazardous’. Lahore ranked as the world’s most polluted city on Friday, with its air quality classified as “hazardous”, according to air quality monitoring platform IQAir. In the past few years, air pollution has become one of the most pressing public health and environmental crises facing Pakistan. Various cities of the country, most notably Lahore , deal with smog, especially in the winter months. The phenomenon is attributed mainly to industrial emissions, vehicular pollution , stubble burning and air movement . Lahore topped the list of the world’s most polluted cities on Friday morning, with an air quality index (AQI) of 410, according to the IQAir live tracker. The reading fell under the ‘very unhealthy’ category. India’s New Delhi followed with an AQI of 203, while Senegal’s Dakar ranked third at 196. Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities according to IQAir on Friday morning. — Screengrab via IQAir The provincial capital was the only Pakistani city to rank among the 20 most polluted cities on Friday morning. Karachi was the only other Pakistani city on the 21-city list, with an AQI of 110. According to IQAir, in Lahore , “PM2.5 concentration is currently 45.2 times the World Health Organisation annual PM2.5 guideline value”. PM2.5 refers to fine inhalable particles, with diameters generally 2.5 micrometres and smaller. Of all air pollution measures, PM2.5 pollution poses the greatest health threat, according to IQAir. According to the website, PM2.5 can enter the circulatory system and even the brain, causing serious health complications if long-term exposure occurs. A view of the early morning in Lahore on Friday. Photo by Murtaza Ali For those in Lahore, IQAir recommended avoiding outdoor exercise, keeping windows closed to prevent outdoor air from entering, wearing a mask outdoors and installing an air purifier indoors. Lahore air quality map. —IQAir The Punjab government’s air quality monitoring platform, meanwhile, recorded an AQI of 339 for Lahore at 11am on Thursday, classifying the air as ‘very unhealthy’. The reading was based on data from 10 monitoring stations across the city. The difference between the readings on the two platforms may be due to variations in monitoring stations, averaging periods and methodologies. However, both indicated severe air pollution in the provincial capital. Human rights activist Sheikh Saqib told Dawn that both his children were suffering from throat infections due to smog. He criticised the government for what he described as empty claims about measures to curb air pollution. A view of the early morning in Lahore on Friday. Photo by Murtaza Ali He said school attendance could drop by half as parents stopped sending their children to school amid deteriorating air quality. Saqib also disputed the chief minister’s claims that smog had been controlled over the past three years, saying he continued to witness crop burning while travelling on motorways towards Islamabad and Karachi. “Vehicles emitting smoke are still running on Lahore’s roads,” he said, questioning the effectiveness of the government’s measures to tackle air pollution. On Oct 2, Lahore also topped IQAir’s list of the world’s most polluted cities, with an AQI of 167, classified as “unhealthy”. At the time, CM Maryam said the government was making efforts to address environmental issues. Earlier this week, a new analysis released by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) ranked Lahore among cities whose ozone levels were “extremely poor”.

Apple launches into foldable market as iPhone Duo sales begin. Sales of Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo , began on Friday, with market watchers betting on whether the device can reinvent the small foldables market in the same way the iPhone did for smartphones. The Duo’s reception could prove an early test for new CEO John Ternus , the former hardware chief who unveiled the phone barely a week after taking charge in September. It could also have large implications for a niche category in which ⁠rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium ​offerings for several years. Within minutes of pre-orders opening last Friday, Apple’s estimated delivery dates for the Duo had slipped to late January as demand outpaced supply. The US company called the response from customers “nothing short of extraordinary.” With the massive demand, Apple capped pre-orders at two handsets per customer and limited sales significantly for walk-in shoppers, resulting in muted crowds unlike the hype that typically accompanied new iPhone releases. In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online In Sydney, the first Apple store to sell the phones on Friday, a queue of customers formed outside before opening at 8am local time (2100 GMT or 2am PKT). Simon Krishnan, a 48-year-old engineer, paid A$3,899 ($2,734) for a Duo with 512GB memory. “This is a bit of a luxury item for me, because it’s so expensive, but I just think, you know what? Life’s too short,” he said. In China, a soft consumer market combined with memory costs pushing prices higher has led to six straight quarters of declines in smartphone shipments. Apple’s market share, however, has rebounded as some phone buyers trade up to premium devices while others seek value at the lower end of the market, putting pressure on mid-range brands. Liu Wei, a 26-year-old healthcare professional, already has a foldable phone from Xiaomi, but still queued outside a central Shanghai Apple store from 6am to get his hands on Apple’s first foldable. “I’ve used Apple products for many years and I have more trust (in the brand), so I bought one on launch day to try it out,” he said. In Hong Kong, May, 38, who declined to give his full name for privacy reasons, secured a 256GB iPhone Duo, which retails for HK$17,499 ($2,231.73), during an online pre‑sale and aimed to resell the handset for a profit of around HK$4,000: “A few meals’ worth of money,” he joked. People use the new foldable iPhone Duo, on its launch day at an Apple store, in Berlin, Germany, on October 23, 2026. — Reuters Mixed reviews Early reviews have praised the Duo’s design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers. But reviewers have said camera compromises including the absence of a telephoto lens and third-party apps that still need to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They have also said the Duo in its smaller, folded state is less handy for the litany of quick tasks that most users carry out each day on standard iPhones, with several prominent reviewers recommending against the Duo for many Apple customers. “It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype — not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry,” longtime Apple commentator John Gruber, author of the blog Daring Fireball , wrote in a review. Tech commentator Marques Brownlee, popularly known as MKBHD , said in a YouTube review that “if you’re just a regular person who doesn’t do much more than texting, social media and browsing here and there, then it is probably a no. But if the $2,000 doesn’t mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone.” People use the new foldable iPhone Duo, on its launch day at an Apple store, in Berlin, Germany, on October 23, 2026. — Reuters Tough to find The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo. Apple told Reuters that walk-in availability would vary by country, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe. “Foldables have been an established category for years, but adoption has remained relatively limited compared with conventional smartphones. Apple’s entry could bring the format to a much broader audience,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president at market researcher IDC. IDC expects Apple will take 44 per cent of the foldable value in 2026 on 31pc of foldable units. By 2027, it will become the market leader in the category both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast. “Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor,” Jeronimo said after spending a week with the passport-shaped Duo. “Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market,” Jeronimo said.

West Bank attack wounds 5 Israelis as Netanyahu cancels events. An attack in the occupied West Bank wounded at least five Israelis on Friday and triggered a shootout that left two Palestinians dead, prompting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to cancel political events days ahead of elections. An AFP journalist who witnessed the firefight saw two Palestinian men in casual attire and armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city of Hebron. The journalist reported that Israeli forces eventually shot and killed the attackers. The Israeli military said soldiers had rushed to the Judea Junction area, also known as the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint, after the early-morning shooting attack. “Israel Defence Forces (IDF) soldiers eliminated two terrorists and continue searches in the area,” it claimed in a statement. Netanyahu claimed Israel had prevented a “major attack” after soldiers killed the two armed Palestinians. He added that he had instructed the military to “impose a cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full closure of the entire West Bank starting today”. Open-source Telegram groups reported that many checkpoints in the area had already been closed The initial shooting wounded five people, two of whom were in critical condition, said Magen David Adom, Israel’s emergency medical rescue service. The Magen David Adom said one of the victims was a man in his 20s in “very serious condition” with gunshot wounds. Netanyahu, running for a new term in elections on Tuesday, called for all political meetings to be cancelled Friday due to the attack. Israeli National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir, who has been rising in the polls, called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be dismantled because of the attack. No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian government in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was connected to Friday’s attack. Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the election, praised the response by troops. “Like all Israelis, I pray for the complete and quick recovery of the injured,” he said. The incident comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters , and days ahead of Israeli elections. According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,113 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023. Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period.

China orders 'all-out' rescue after Tibet quake kills 16. China ordered an “all-out” rescue effort in Tibet on Friday after an earthquake killed at least 16 people, injured dozens and flattened hundreds of homes, state media reported. Footage showed rescue workers with torches clambering in the dark through some of the more than 300 houses that Xinhua said collapsed in the 7.0-magnitude quake on Thursday evening. Diners ran out of restaurants and items fell off wobbling supermarket shelves as the tremor struck, according to clips on state broadcaster CCTV , which said 65 people were injured. One resident told local media that her family had just gone to bed when her home shook, knocking over objects, and that they “rushed outside without even taking the time to get dressed.” “My legs were shaking the entire time I was heading downstairs and by the time I reached the bottom, I was so terrified that I burst into tears,” the woman said. Local residents “are afraid to return to their homes,” she said. “They set up tents along the roadside or spent the night in their cars.” A man told the Beijing News that the “very strong” quake left his home “creaking and rattling”. “I was asleep when it hit. Everyone has run outside now and is too afraid to go back in. I’m currently driving to an open area to sleep in my car,” he said. Broadcaster CCTV also showed emergency personnel with helmets carrying a person and shining flashlights on damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs. Tibet is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists and Chinese authorities are the only source of official information. ‘Significant casualties’ President Xi Jinping said the tremor caused “significant casualties” and took place at a “high-altitude location” in cold weather. “(We) must go all-out to carry out search and rescue operations and do our utmost to treat the injured, so as to minimise casualties,” Xinhua quoted Xi as saying. He called for assistance for residents and rescue equipment to be sent to the area promptly. The epicentre was in a mountainous area about 190 kilometres east-northeast of Nagqu, and 390 kilometres northeast of the regional capital Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said. It struck at 10:33 pm (7:33 pm PKT) on Thursday at a shallow depth of around 10 kilometres. Lhawang Dagpo, a local official in the Maru township, the quake’s epicentre, said it put cracks in the walls of his office, according to Xinhua . Power and telecoms services were disrupted in the county seat, the agency said. Baqing County has mobilised more than 1,600 people to help in the relief operation, CCTV reported. The municipal fire and rescue brigade has dispatched 25 vehicles and 110 personnel, and the Nagqu Armed Police Detachment sent 225 officers and soldiers and 18 vehicles, CCTV said. As of 4:30 am (1:30 am PKT) on Friday, relief supplies including 1,000 prefabricated houses, 3,239 tents, four generators and 1,000 flashlights had been delivered, it added. President Zardari, PM Shehbaz extend condolences President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, in separate statements on Friday, extended their condolences to the Chinese president, the bereaved families and the people of China. Both leaders also reaffirmed Pakistan’s solidarity with China and prayed for the swift recovery of those injured. In a statement shared by his office, President Zardari “expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives”. PM Shehbaz said he was deeply saddened by “the tragic loss of precious lives and injuries caused by the devastating earthquake”. He added that Pakistan was “ready to extend every possible support”. Earthquakes in China are relatively common. In January 2025, a quake in Tibet’s rural Tingri county killed at least 126 people. The disaster came little over a year after at least 148 people died in a quake in remote Gansu province in northwest China in December 2023, according to state media. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people perished in the southwestern province of Yunnan . A massive tremor in 2008 in Sichuan province left about 90,000 people dead or missing, including around thousands of schoolchildren.

‘Hit them hard’: CDF Munir vows to continue campaign against Indian-sponsored terrorist outfits. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir has said the armed forces will continue the counterterrorism campaign against Indian-sponsored terrorist groups “to the fullest”, vowing to “hit them hard wherever they are”, the military’s media wing said on Friday. CDF Munir made the remarks during a visit to the Corps Headquarters in Peshawar, where he was briefed on the security situation, ongoing counterterrorism operations, border management measures and the operational preparedness of formations deployed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. Upon arrival at the headquarters, CDF Munir was received by the Peshawar Corps commander. During his visit, he lauded the morale and professionalism of the armed forces and directed them to maintain “vigilance and the highest standards of operational readiness to effectively counter threats”. ISPR added that CDF Munir vowed that the armed forces would “continue the campaign against Indian-sponsored terrorist outfits to the fullest and hit them hard wherever they are”. He also paid tribute to the martyred security personnel, affirming that “with the support of the people, Pakistan will surely inflict total defeat on the terrorists and their perverted ideology”. A day earlier, CDF Munir attended a meeting of KP apex committee held at the Governor House, where the province’s overall security situation was reviewed. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif who chaired the meeting, said that the federal government, which now runs KP under governor’s rule, would make every effort possible to “bring back” progress to the province. According to a recent report from the Centre for Research and Security Studies, Pakistan recorded a sharp 83 per cent increase in violence-linked fatalities during the third quarter of 2026, reversing a declining trend reported in the first and second quarters as terrorism and counter-terrorism deaths surged nationwide. Balochistan and KP remained the epicentres of violence, jointly accounting for 98pc of all fatalities during the period. Balochistan recorded 829 deaths, nearly 59pc of the national total, while KP reported 556 fatalities, accounting for more than 39pc. The increased terrorist activity has prompted security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. A day earlier, four policemen, including two officials, were martyred and two terrorists were killed during an exchange of fire in KP’s Karak. On October 19, an army major was martyred and four terrorists were killed during intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan. A day before that, security forces killed eight “India-sponsored” terrorists during IBOs conducted in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan.

New Greece law bans social media for under-15s. Greece’s parliament passed a law on Friday banning children under 15 from social media, joining a growing number of countries imposing curbs on young people’s use of the apps. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced plans for the ban in April, taking to TikTok — one of the most popular social networks with young people in Greece — to explain the “difficult but necessary” measure. After a heated debate in a parliamentary session that started on Thursday and stretched into Friday, Mitsotakis’s conservative New Democracy party used its majority to pass the bill, which no other parties backed, the Ana news agency reported. The opposition socialist Pasok party abstained after seeking an alternative bill that would have banned social media for under-13s and parental controls for 13- and 14-year-olds. Other left-wing and nationalist parties voted against. The bill, set to take effect on January 1, will require age verification on social networks and impose harsh penalties if companies fail to comply. Australia last year became the first country to introduce such a social media ban for kids, barring under-16s. More than 20 countries have passed similar laws, according to an AFP tally. Critics say social networks use addictive algorithms to keep kids glued to their screens, and warn excessive scrolling can damage their mental health. Bans have faced pushback from free-speech advocates, and sceptics question how well they will work.

Insulin product in short supply after German manufacturer halts supplies, NA told. An insulin product used by patients with Type 1 diabetes is in short supply in Pakistan after its German manufacturer halted supplies while upgrading its products, Parliamentary Secretary for Health Nelson Azeem said on Friday. Responding to a matter raised by MNA Syeda Amna Batool in the National Assembly, Azeem said there had been no shortage until June, with stocks available until September. However, supplies from Germany were disrupted in October, leading to the current shortage. “The impact of the shortage is being felt not just here, but across Asia, as well as in Australia and Europe,” Azeem said. “The product will be available as soon as international supplies are restored.” The secretary further said alternative insulin products with the same dosage and mode of action were readily available in Pakistan and that patients could switch to them on their doctors’ recommendation. “The product is manufactured in Germany. It is an issue that we are trying to resolve,” he said. However, Batool expressed concern about the difficulties patients could face in switching treatments. She said the alternatives were at least 20 per cent more expensive and that many patients did not have access to doctors. “Currently, around 34.5 million people in Pakistan have Type 1 diabetes, including children,” she said. “Alternatives are not readily available. Has the health ministry or the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (Drap) ensured their easy availability?” Azeem asserted the German manufacturer had previously supplied 3,500 kits, but supplies had now fallen to 1,000 kits and could decline further during the year-long upgrade process. He said the health ministry had asked distributors importing the product to arrange supplies, but acknowledged that this would be difficult because the manufacturer had halted production. On Tuesday, authorities had denied reports of a widespread insulin shortage in the country, saying that only one brand was unavailable. “Insulin glulisine (Apidra, Sanofi) is currently unavailable due to international supply constraints. Alternate rapid-acting analogues within the same pharmacological class, specifically insulin aspart (NovoRapid, Novo Nordisk) and insulin lispro (Humalog, Eli Lilly), are readily available nationwide,” health ministry spokesperson Sajid Shah had said, adding that all other primary insulin classes remained fully accessible across Pakistan. In August 2025, the Pakistan Medical Association raised alarm over “an unprecedented” and severe shortage of essential medicines across the country and warned that the crisis threatened the lives of millions of patients. According to the association, at least 80 important medicines were unavailable, with 25 having no substitutes. These drugs included life-saving medications for diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, heart disease and psychiatric disorders.

The Gulf’s emerging web of security partnerships. The signing of the Badr Memorandum of Understanding by Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar and Indonesia in Doha on Wednesday is the latest manifestation of Middle Eastern states accelerated efforts for diversifying their defense partnerships amid growing doubts about the reliability of existing security arrangements of the region led by the United States. But, rather than laying the foundations of a new regional security architecture, the proliferation of such agreements is producing a more fractured landscape in which countries are drawing in more partners, pursuing separate strategic interests and accepting varying levels of military commitments. There could not be a bigger example of how uneven is the process than the agreements being signed up by regional countries themselves. Badr , for instance, focuses on defense manufacturing, technology transfer, research and development, and training, allowing its participants to pool industrial capabilities without committing themselves to military assistance in the event of an attack. In contrast the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement , concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, goes considerably further by providing that an attack on one participant will be treated as an attack on all as it builds on a bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement between Pakistan and KSA signed in Sept 2025. These are two major agreements in addition to several others being signed or solidified by the countries in the region, but the contrast between Badr and Makkah agreements is telling because these agreements are often taken as evidence of an emerging regional security architecture, although the arrangements differ considerably in their purpose and obligations. Makkah agreement formalises security guarantees between participating countries, while Badr aims to develop industrial capacity. The momentum behind these regional security initiatives has grown since this year’s US - Israel war with Iran exposed the risks of relying heavily on external protection. For Gulf states in particular, the Iran conflict raised questions about whether existing security partnerships could adequately protect their interests during a major regional confrontation. Importantly, the response of the affected countries has not been to abandon US, whose military capabilities are still considered indispensable, but to seek additional options through new partnerships, domestic defense production and selective commitments. Besides the impression of the inadequacy of US security umbrella, this search for greater strategic autonomy also needs to be looked at in the context of the Gulf Cooperation Council’s own Joint Defense Agreement, signed in 2000, which too provides that aggression against one member constitutes aggression against all, yet the bloc has struggled to translate this commitment into an integrated military capability because of differences in equipment, command systems and national priorities. The hurdles to full operationalisation of Peninsula Shield Force has further exposed the gap between a collective defense principle and the ability to organise a coordinated response. The newer arrangements that the countries in the region are signing up partly reflect this GCC experience. Therefore, while these countries want enhanced security cooperation, they are also reluctant to surrender the freedom to make independent decisions. As a result, a network of partnerships is emerging that may complement one another in some areas without actually adding up to a common defense system. Pakistan’s expanding role illustrates both the opportunities and the limitations of this approach. Its relationship with Saudi Arabia has acquired a more formal security dimension through the 2025 bilateral agreement and the subsequent Makkah framework, while cooperation with Turkiye offers scope for closer military coordination and defense industrial collaboration. Egypt, another key player in the Arab world, has stayed outside the Makkah framework and has offered defense cooperation to Saudi Arabia, reflecting its interest in protecting its own regional priorities without becoming committed to a wider military confrontation. Islamabad’s other Gulf relationships, however, remain more limited in scope. Kuwait has strengthened defense cooperation with Pakistan through an upgraded agreement - the Protocol Agreement 2026 - covering training, capacity building and border management, while Bahrain has developed close links with the Pakistani military through the presence of Pakistani personnel in its National Guard and Coast Guard, alongside cooperation in training and logistics. These relationships have provided a basis for continued military engagement but do not carry the mutual defense obligations associated with the Pakistan - KSA partnership. Ties with UAE have, meanwhile, followed a more complicated course marred by political and financial strains, Islamabad’s closer alignment with Riyadh and Abu Dhabi’s expanding defense relationship with India. Nevertheless, training, personnel exchanges, counterterrorism activities and joint exercises between the two countries continue. Qatar has signed a defense industrial cooperation agreement involving Pakistan among others while Oman has maintained selective military ties with Pakistan and Turkiye, simultaneously preserving its wider security relationships and avoiding binding mutual defense commitments, consistent with its preference for neutrality and diplomatic engagement, particularly in relation to Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. This makes it difficult to describe Pakistan’s growing defense relationships as a unified regional bloc. Moreover, commitments under these agreements vary according to the interests and calculations of individual partners. Islamabad, in this situation, is left to balance closer security ties against its available military resources and the risk of becoming involved in conflicts whose objectives may not coincide with its own. At the same time the Gulf states are also pursuing different courses. Saudi Arabia is strengthening its relationships with Pakistan and Turkiye while continuing to rely on Western military capabilities and Egypt and exploring defense industrial cooperation with China. The UAE, which has not joined either the Makkah or Badr frameworks, has deepened security cooperation with Israel, including in air defense and counter drone capabilities, while maintaining close relationships with US, France and India. Qatar is seeking to expand its defense industrial partnerships through Badr but at the same time retains US military presence at Al Udeid. Bahrain remains closely aligned with Saudi Arabia and the GCC defense framework, while Kuwait continues to prioritise bilateral military cooperation with Pakistan alongside its substantial security relationship with Washington. Oman’s preference for neutrality and mediation further distinguishes its approach from those seeking more formal security commitments. The differences are not only confined to the choice of partners, but the states also have divergent assessments of the threat posed by Iran, the role of Israel in regional security and the degree to which they should commit themselves to one another’s defense. Their partnerships are therefore being shaped as much by the need to preserve freedom of action as by the desire to develop collective capabilities. The new partnerships do not either automatically translate into military independence for regional states, which continue to operate substantial inventories of Western origin aircraft, air defense systems and other advanced platforms that require specialised maintenance, software support, spare parts and replacement munitions. New partners may help diversify procurement and develop local production, but they cannot necessarily replace established suppliers on the required scale. Moreover, addition of newer systems can also complicate logistics and interoperability unless countries invest in common procedures, training and secure communications. Defense industrial cooperation presents another challenge and agreements such as Badr will acquire practical significance only if they lead to funded production programs, meaningful technology transfer and capabilities that participating countries can maintain and sustain. Similarly, the credibility of mutual defense arrangements will depend on whether their members can coordinate intelligence, plan jointly and establish procedures for responding to a crisis. The number of agreements signed, therefore, is less important than the military capabilities and obligations they actually produce. For Washington, this proliferation of new defense agreements may apparently look like a challenge, but this should definitely not be seen as it being replaced. US undoubtedly remains deeply embedded in the region through military bases, intelligence cooperation, arms sales and longstanding defense relationships. The emerging shift may, however, give the regional countries greater bargaining power with established suppliers, particularly as they press for domestic production, technology partnerships and greater control over maintenance and supply chains. To put it simply the emerging arrangements are an attempt to manage the uncertainty created by recent geo-political developments especially the receding US footprint rather than replace the existing system outright. The central contradiction in the Gulf countries response to the emerging situation, however, is that while these states are seeking greater security through a proliferation of partnerships, they remain unwilling, or unable, to reconcile their differences over the threats they face and the obligations they are prepared to assume.

State counsel cross-examines prosecution witnesses in security breach case against Imaan, Hadi. ISLAMABAD: A state-appointed counsel on Friday cross-examined all prosecution witnesses in a security breach case against lawyers Imaan Zainab Hazir-Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha. Imaan and her husband, Hadi, are facing a jail trial in a 2024 case pertaining to the alleged disruption of an international cricket team’s security route and incitement to public unrest. The couple, accused of removing barriers from the route, was indicted on Oct 7. Anti-terrorism court Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra presided over the hearing held inside Adiala jail on Friday, during which state counsel Atif Mehmood cross-examined a prosecution witness. On Saturday, the court will provide Imaan and Hadi with questionnaires under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to record their statements. In a hearing on Thursday, the court appointed Mehmood as the state counsel to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses, replacing Taimoor Janjua, who was dismissed over his past conduct. The court had ruled to appoint the state attorney after the defence counsel failed to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses. During the last hearing, Imaan informed the court that she and Hadi did not need a state counsel as they already had their own lawyers. Hadi explained that their lawyers were frequently occupied with other cases at the Islamabad High Court (IHC), while the trial court had scheduled daily hearings at Adiala, making it difficult for them to attend every proceeding. The court had directed the prosecution witnesses to appear again on Friday, affirming that the cross-examination would proceed without further delay. Imaan and Hadi’s rearrest The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the IHC and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in the controversial social media posts case. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and Hadi were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

10 India-sponsored terrorists killed as bid to undermine state's writ in Gwadar foiled: ISPR. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Friday that 10 India-sponsored terrorists were killed in separate engagements as security forces thwarted their attempts to “undermine the writ of the state” in Balochistan’s Gwadar district. In a statement, the military’s media affairs wing said: “On Oct 22, Indian-sponsored terrorists of Fitna al Hindustan attempted to carry out terrorist activities in district Gwadar, in the general areas of the Gabd Border Crossing and Gwadar city.” The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. “By targeting these locations, terrorists sought to harm the very people they claim to represent and wanted to obstruct the development and prosperity of Balochistan. To protect residents and clear the area, security forces launched clearance operations in and around Gwadar city,” ISPR said. It said that in separate engagements, security forces foiled the terrorists’ designs and “their bid to undermine the writ of the state and spread their misconstrued agenda”. “In the ensuing exchanges of fire, ten terrorists, including one female terrorist, were sent to hell. During the terrorist attacks one civilian embraced shahadat (martyrdom) and [a] few vehicles were damaged. Operations were concluded without any loss to security forces, restoring order and writ of the state,” it said. The statement further said that the coercion of a Baloch woman into the attack was “a crime not only against the state but against the hurmat (respect) of Baloch women”. “It exposes the terrorists’ cynical exploitation of Baloch women as an instrument of propaganda, intended to inflame public sentiment and lend false sanctity to their campaign. Such tactics are contrary to Baloch and Islamic traditions, which hold women in the highest honour. The people of Balochistan have consistently rejected those who shed blood in their name, and they will see through this deception as well,” it said. The statement said that the counterterror campaign would continue at full pace. “Security forces and law enforcement agencies remain resolute in eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country,” it said. The ISPR statement comes a day after security sources said that security forces killed three terrorists and foiled an attack on an unoccupied construction company camp in Gwadar. Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir said earlier on Friday the armed forces will continue the counterterrorism campaign against Indian-sponsored terrorist groups “to the fullest”, vowing to “hit them hard wherever they are”. Earlier this week, ISPR said an army major was martyred and four terrorists were killed during intelligence-based operations in Balochistan. The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August , according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). As per the report, Balochistan was declared the province “most affected” by terrorism. Following the latest operations by security forces in Gwadar, President Asif Ali Zardari commended the security forces for foiling the terrorists’ attempts. “The president also expressed deep sorrow and grief over the martyrdom of a citizen in a terrorism incident,” the statement issued by the Presidency said. It further quoted President Zardari as saying that efforts to disrupt peace and stability in Balochistan could not shake the people’s resolve for development and prosperity in the province. He stressed the importance of peace for the protection of the rights and interests of people of Balochistan and said that “using the honour of Baloch women for political interests is condemnable”.

DPM Dar meets Turkish FM ahead of R-4 bloc, European diplomats’ meetings. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Friday met with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, ahead of a meeting of R-4 foreign ministers and a meeting between the R-4 and European diplomats, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The R-4 group, comprising Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, emerged in March and has been focusing on regional security and mediation efforts between the United States and Iran. In a post on X, the FO said that Dar thanked Fidan for hosting the meetings and that the pair discussed bilateral relations and regional developments, particularly the situation in the Middle East and Palestine. “They expressed concern over threats to regional stability and underscored the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and coordinated efforts to promote regional peace and security,” the FO post said. Additionally, Dar and Fidan strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their commitment to close coordination on regional issues, including under the Makkah Defence Agreement. “Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship and brotherhood between Pakistan and Turkiye, and to deepening cooperation across all areas of mutual interest, both bilaterally and in multilateral fora,” the FO added. Dar left for Istanbul earlier in the day and is attending the meeting at the invitation of Fidan. In a post on X, the FO said that upon his arrival, Dar arrived in Istanbul and was received by Director General of the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs Cihad Erginay and Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires Shaiq Ahmed. The FO added that during his one-day visit, Deputy Prime Minister (DPM) Dar would participate in the R-4 and R-4-plus meetings with France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom. Dar would also call on Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts, the FO said. Earlier, FO said that the ministers will participate in a meeting with counterparts from the European E-3 bloc — UK, France, and Germany — following the R-4 meeting. The E-3 group comprises three European powers that established the grouping more than 20 years ago to advance diplomatic coordination on Iran’s nuclear programme. Italy will also be a part of the meeting, FO had added. “This will be the first meeting of the seven countries in this format,” FO said. “The meetings will focus on key regional developments and explore coordinated diplomatic approaches to address shared challenges and advance regional peace and stability,” FO added. DPM Dar is also set to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts during his visit as well. “Pakistan’s participation reflects its continued commitment to constructive diplomacy, regional cooperation and the peaceful resolution of disputes,” FO said. Talks to revolve around Hormuz, Saudi Arabia British foreign minister Ed Miliband’s office said the talks would essentially revolve around “the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia”. It said Miliband “will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the (Hormuz) crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms”. He will also stress “how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilising the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab El-Mandeb and the Suez Canal”, it added. France confirmed the talks on “the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications”, hailing it as a first “in this format… against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region.” The meeting will aim to “strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all,” the French foreign ministry said. A Turkish diplomatic source also told Reuters a day earlier that the seven countries would meet in the R-4+E-3 format for the first time at Turkiye’s initiative as wars involving Iran , Yemen and Ukraine threaten shipping routes and regional security. Fidan is expected to emphasise the need for a diplomatic solution to the war between the United States and Iran, the importance of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, and reiterate Turkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security against attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed by Islamabad, Ankara, and Riyadh, the sources said. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

At least 12 killed, 22 injured in road accident near Zero Point in Balochistan’s Uthal. KHUZDAR: At least 12 passengers were killed and around two dozen injured when a minibus and a passenger coach collided head-on near Zero Point in Uthal on the Quetta-Karachi Highway in Balochistan on Friday, police said. According to police, the coach was travelling from Gwadar to Karachi, while the minibus was heading from Bela to Karachi. “The tragic incident took place near Bela when the passenger coach hit the minibus,” the officials said, adding that seven passengers were killed on the spot, while five others succumbed to their injuries in hospital. In-charge of the Edhi Centre in Bela Abdul Hakeem Lasi said around 22 injured passengers were shifted to hospital by Edhi workers before being taken to Karachi for treatment. He said seven injured passengers were in serious condition. Most of the casualties occurred in the minibus, he added. The accident occurred two days after 10 people were killed and 44 others injured when a passenger bus overturned after hitting a road divider in Rajanpur district’s Rojhan tehsil on the Indus Highway on Wednesday. A similar accident occurred last month when two people were killed and 15 others injured in a head-on collision between a passenger coach and an LPG bowser near Balochistan’s Kharkhera Customs on the main National Highway in Winder. In February, five people, including a local journalist, were killed in two separate road accidents in Winder and Khuzdar districts. In January, four people were killed and several others injured in a road accident near Wadh in Khuzdar district on the Quetta-Karachi National Highway.

Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin mloukili Thu, 10/15/2026 - 14:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Commentary / Europe 15 October 2026 12 minutes Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin Criminal groups have taken over swathes of the Amazon, fuelling violence and environmental destruction through illicit business. In this excerpt from the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group shows how the EU and member states can curb these activities and ecological damage. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Download PDF Full Report Download Full Report Select your download language English Spanish Also available in Español Español English Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union Amazon The Amazon, the world’s largest tropical rainforest, is vital for planetary wellbeing. But it is also the source of several commodities, often obtained and sold illegally, that are in high commercial demand. Expanding markets for gold, wood, beef, critical minerals, wildlife, soy and cocaine, among other licit and illicit goods, have resulted in widespread environmental harm, including deforestation and contamination of soil and waterways . The alarming result is that parts of the Amazon are now releasing more carbon into the atmosphere than they absorb, contributing to global warming. Meanwhile, the crime rings involved in supplying some of these items have tightened their grip on swathes of the Amazon , particularly its rivers and estuaries. The profits they reap allow them to challenge state authority and co-opt officials. They use lethal violence against Indigenous and other residents to consolidate their hold. Europe is a major destination for many of the Amazon’s illicit or illegally produced goods. It is also at the forefront of efforts to contain global climate change, a cause that depends for its success on preserving ecosystems such as the Amazon. Yet European governments have been hesitant to address the intersection of trafficking and organised crime in the Amazon, which makes the job of preserving the rainforest much harder. The EU and its member states should work closely with South American partners to improve security cooperation, harmonise legal norms around environmental crimes, back Indigenous community responses aimed at curtailing illicit businesses and support the creation of legal livelihoods in the Amazon. This set of initiatives could help weaken the criminal groups bringing violence to the Amazon and limit the environmental damage they cause. Aerial view taken during a Greenpeace flyover of illegal mining areas in Kayapo indigenous territory in Para state, Brazil, on 19 March, 2025. AFP / Pablo Porciuncula Organised Crime in the Jungle Over the last decade, criminal groups have extended their reach across the Amazon, both to exploit its natural riches and to use its rivers to carry goods to seaports for shipment to European and Asian buyers. Governments in the Amazon basin have taken action to stop these activities, seeking to curb both the environmental degradation they cause and the attendant violence, but shifting political priorities and lack of resources have meant that the effects of their campaigns have been uneven. Criminals take advantage of discrepancies among the various countries’ penal codes to avoid running afoul of regulations and facing prosecution. For instance, Brazil prohibits the commercial export of many wildlife species, while Guyana and Suriname permit it under a quota. As a result, traffickers can catch animals in Brazil, move them across one of the borders and ship them legally from Guyana and Suriname without needing to forge documents. Shifting Drug Routes Drug traffickers have long taken advantage of the Amazon’s vast expanses and weak state presence to cultivate and process coca crops and transport cocaine, which they then send across the Atlantic Ocean. Despite prohibition measures, South American production of the narcotic is at an all-time high, spurred by a boom in consumption in Europe. In response, Europe has continued to focus its law enforcement efforts on drug interdictions , largely as shipments approach the continent’s ports. The U.S., for its part, has turned to military firepower, launching a wave of attacks on alleged drug-carrying boats along routes across the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, killing almost 240 suspected traffickers so far. Some reports claim that these U.S. strikes have pushed additional quantities of drugs onto Amazon routes, but more research is needed to verify such a shift. That said, evidence does show that drug markets in the rainforest are more robust than ever: in Brazil alone, there was a 574 per cent increase in cocaine seizures in the country’s nine Amazon basin states between 2019 and 2024. With the state’s reach limited in much of the Amazon, traffickers move cocaine from Bolivia, Colombia and Peru to ports in the Guianas and Brazil. Barcarena, where the Amazon empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Source: Crisis Group research; OpenStreetMap / CRISIS GROUP The limited reach of the state in much of the Amazon means that traffickers face few obstacles in transporting cocaine, which is produced mostly in Bolivia, Colombia and Peru, to ports in the Guianas (as the north-eastern part of South America comprising French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname is known) and Brazil, from where they ship it to Europe, either directly or via West Africa . Barcarena, the Brazilian town where the Amazon river system empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Cocaine leaves through the Vila do Conde container terminal concealed in legitimate cargo, usually without the exporter’s knowledge. Recent shipments have been found in açaí , quartz and soy meal consignments bound for Portugal, the Netherlands, France and Australia. Crisis Group has previously written about how criminal groups in the region collaborate, with each playing a role in transforming coca into cocaine, moving it through the Amazon and distributing it worldwide. These networks encompass Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho in Brazil; the National Liberation Army or ELN, Comandos de la Frontera and other FARC dissident groups in Colombia; and Los Lobos and Los Choneros in Ecuador. All these organisations have employed violence and payoffs to quash local resistance and rid themselves of state agents who get in the way of doing business. But, reflecting what is happening elsewhere in Latin America, competition among criminal groups in the Amazon is also becoming lethal. Along the Orinoco River and Río Negro, shared by Colombia and Venezuela, a long-time alliance between the ELN and FARC dissidents of the Segunda Marquetalia came to an end in August 2025 , triggering clashes in which the groups used landmines and drones. As rivals jostle for control of markets, violence is likely to get worse. The expansion of organised crime is particularly pernicious for young residents of areas where they operate. These groups often hire children and adolescents to help with logistical tasks, paying them in drugs rather than cash. The kids then sell the drugs, causing substance abuse to rise in riverine villages. Along the Amazon River in Colombia, for example, Indigenous Ticuna people report that drug sale points have cropped up in rural areas. With no harm reduction programs in place, elders worry about the future of their children and the long-term effects on their communities. Gold and Other Commodities Many drug trafficking organisations have diversified into illegal gold mining, as rising prices for the metal have made it lucrative , with sales often raking in more income for criminals than cocaine. Illicit gold extraction can destroy ecosystems, as miners raze forests and pollute rivers and their banks with mercury (used to separate bits of gold from sediment). Mining sites have also been linked to grave human rights abuses, including violence against Indigenous leaders, sexual exploitation and child labour. Besides being highly profitable, gold is appealing because the product itself is easily transported and difficult to trace to its source. Even if illegally extracted, it can be funnelled into the legal supply chain at little risk just by forging paperwork. Criminal organisations seize this opportunity to “clean” drug trafficking proceeds by either investing in illegal gold mining or purchasing gold directly. The Guianas are a hub for these practices, as local regulations allow miners to absorb gold extracted in Venezuela and then re-export it as if it was locally produced. Over the past decade, much of Venezuela’s illicit gold has reached Switzerland and Belgium in this way , with large quantities also transiting Amsterdam. Security forces throughout the Amazon region are also concerned about Venezuela’s growing role in laundering illegal gold from Brazil and Colombia. After Caracas adopted a new mining law and U.S. sanctions authorities provided a licence for sales from the state company Minerven, illicit gold sellers have sought to mix their products into this newly legal pipeline for international sales. Law enforcement officials have told Crisis Group that “dirty gold” from other Amazon countries often passes through European airports for sale to refiners and minerals traders in countries including Germany and Italy. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. The ELN-Segunda Marquetalia fighting, which has spread from Venezuela into Colombia, was sparked by contests over gold and critical mineral mining sites as well as narcotics. In April, for example, these two groups battled in the Venezuelan municipality of Cedeño, displacing dozens of families . Other coveted minerals can also be found in the Amazon, including coltan, tin and tungsten. More than half the world’s critical mineral deposits are located on or in proximity to Indigenous lands. In Brazil, for instance, companies have sought permission to look for critical minerals in or near almost 44 per cent of the country’s Indigenous territories. The people residing in remote areas of the rainforest are often the victims of violence and other abuses committed by armed groups undertaking exploration. In Venezuela’s Amazonas and Bolívar states, coltan, tin and tungsten are mined in Indigenous lands that are under guerrilla control ; residents told Crisis Group that child labour, sexual violence and summary executions are frequent. To make matters worse, Venezuelan state forces in the area are reportedly collecting kickbacks from the groups, rather than protecting the vulnerable, and at times enriching themselves by taking more direct control of mines. Meanwhile, cattle ranching, land grabbing and industrial agriculture, the main drivers of Amazon deforestation, continue to grow as criminal groups launder money by investing in land, livestock and agribusiness. In Brazil, the expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching accounted for 99 per cent of native vegetation loss in 2025. What is at Stake for the EU Europe is tied to the violence and environmental damage done by resource extraction and trafficking in the Amazon because it is a major customer for the commodities in question. At the same time, the EU presents itself as a partner in forest protection and sustainable development as ways to mitigate the effects of climate change. But the attention paid by European leaders to the Amazon crisis has been fitful, due partly to sheer distance and partly to preoccupation with more immediate problems like the Ukraine and Middle East wars. European governments are also inclined to avoid engaging with Latin America in ways that might upset the U.S., particularly under the Trump administration, which has made clear it wants Washington to be the dominant influence in the Western Hemisphere. Even in law enforcement cooperation, which Washington seems to favour, Europe is keen to avoid any initiatives resembling U.S. backing for lethal armed force. The health of the rainforest and its inhabitants, however, is crucial for the EU in several ways. In recognition of its importance to achieving Europe’s climate goals, the EU-funded Amazonia+ program currently supports eight Amazon countries in tackling deforestation, forest degradation and wildfires. Germany and France, meanwhile, have pledged up to 1.5 billion euros combined to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a new Brazilian-led fund that pays countries for each hectare of forest they preserve. Furthermore, in March the EU adopted a binding 2040 target of slashing net emissions by 90 per cent from 1990 levels. While at least 85 per cent of that cut must be achieved domestically, up to 5 per cent of the remainder may be met by buying carbon credits from projects outside the EU (each credit will represent one tonne of emissions cut, or carbon removed somewhere else on Europe’s behalf). Cooperating with states and civil society in the Amazon could help meet these objectives. Another issue of acute concern for Europe is critical minerals. The EU and its member states are keen to diversify imports of these minerals , which have important applications in the green, digital, defence and aerospace sectors, and the Amazon is well positioned to form part of its supply chains. At present, Europe relies heavily on China, which builds more than 90 per cent of the world’s rare earth magnets and dominates refining of these elements. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act aims to ensure EU access to a secure and sustainable supply of these materials. Of the 34 minerals on the EU’s critical raw materials list , 25 are extracted in Latin America. Brussels has already established partnerships with two Latin American countries, Argentina and Chile , aimed at boosting cooperation on critical raw mineral extraction, while negotiations with Brazil are under way. Brazil already supplies over 80 per cent of the EU’s niobium, with most of its unprocessed copper coming from Brazil, Peru and Chile. Responsible mining investment in Latin America could help European countries acquire these valuable elements while limiting the harmful consequences for local communities and the environment. The EU has already adopted rules to address concerns about criminal profiteering and abuses in the mineral supply chain. But these are restricted in scope, and some have yet to kick in. The EU’s Conflict Minerals Regulation requires importers to carry out due diligence to guarantee their supply chains are not funding armed groups, violence or abuses, though it applies only to tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold, not the full list of critical raw materials. Another initiative, the Critical Raw Materials Act , allows the EU to fast-track certain projects, so long as they put environmental, social and human rights safeguards in place. Yet only a small subset of projects is covered, and there is too little transparency about which ones are chosen and how to ensure compliance. Enforcement of the landmark Deforestation Regulation, meant to bar soy, cattle, timber and other commodities from the EU market unless proven to have no connection to deforestation, has now been pushed back twice under pressure from industry and trade partners. It is now set to enter force in December. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities. Arguably, however, European states’ main concern is the cocaine pouring into their cities from South America, including via the Amazon trafficking route. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities like Antwerp and Rotterdam, as well as in other hotspots in Italy, Spain, France and Germany. Crisis Group’s conversations with European officials suggest that curbing drug trafficking is a pressing policy concern for many governments and voters. Europe’s efforts to address drug trafficking in Latin America have already touched on the Amazon route, mostly through the now completed COPOLAD program. In Peru, for example, the program funded the creation of an early warning system to flag environmental crimes and criminal threats to human rights defenders. EU cooperation initiatives such as EL PAcCTO 2.0 have also funded projects to boost cross-border law enforcement cooperation on illegal gold mining. In late 2025, EL PAcCTO, Interpol and the Dutch police environmental crime unit aided Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname in the first transnational operation to this effect , known as the Guyana Shield, which resulted in 198 arrests and seizures of illicit goods. Germany, for its part, has long funded the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), while other European countries take part in specific initiatives on security in the region. France, for example, has deployed a liaison officer to the international police cooperation centre in Manaus, Brazil, created following the ACTO’s 2023 Belém Declaration . The EU is also supporting efforts to enhance border management and multinational frontier cooperation as well as to counter human trafficking in Latin America through EUROFRONT , including Amazon-region borders between Colombia and Ecuador. To tackle the challenges facing the Amazon, the EU and its member states should: Help improve law enforcement cooperation and legal harmonisation. The EU and its member states should pair seizures of illicit commodities with asset recovery and money laundering investigations that target the European counterparts of local criminal syndicates. The EU should also step up support for multinational law enforcement and expand port and container security cooperation with Amazon exit points such as Barcarena and the Guianas, where interdiction is weakest and cocaine shipments are on the rise. The EU and its partners should also push for legal harmonisation – eg, of illicit trafficking definitions in various penal codes – within the ACTO and Andean Community. To this end, the EU should support a proposal spearheaded by Brazil to add environmental crimes to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. Strengthen legislation governing gold and critical minerals markets. Critical raw materials refined outside the EU and imported as finished components fall outside the EU’s regulatory frameworks on conflict minerals and deforestation, while unrefined rare earths and bauxite are not covered at all. To ensure that its imports are not linked to criminal activity, the EU, its member states and its partners should support efforts such as those led by Brazil’s Federal Police and Colombia’s geological service to build gold and/or critical mineral traceability systems. The EU should also support law enforcement efforts targeting secondary products used in illicit mining, such as mercury, fuel, cyanide, explosives and mining equipment. Design a holistic approach toward the Amazon. The withdrawal of U.S. development aid has left gaps in environmental support and programming for alternative livelihoods in communities across the Amazon. While Europe cannot completely fill those spaces, the EU should focus support on market access, education and climate adaptation, particularly in coca-growing and gold-mining regions. Global Gateway – the EU’s strategy for financing infrastructure and connectivity projects in partner countries – should channel private investment toward sustainable infrastructure that could help make legal activities such as small-scale farming and fishing more commercially feasible, reducing the incentives for local communities to participate in illicit activity. Simultaneously, to slow deforestation, the EU should double down on results-based strategies such as that of the TFFF, which offers direct benefits to states that succeed in conserving forested areas. Back Indigenous governance. The EU and its member states should encourage capitals across the region to work closely with Indigenous organisations in monitoring illegal activities in remote jungles, since they are well placed to spot criminal activity where state security institutions are weak or absent.
