Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? eschelhaas Thu, 10/15/2026 - 18:12 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Palestinian farmer walks past election banners near the Palestinian-owned olive groves in the village of Rantes near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on October 6, 2026. ZAIN JAAFAR / AFP Q&A / Middle East & North Africa 15 October 2026 16 minutes Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? Israelis will soon head to the polls for the first time since the 7 October 2023 attacks and the seismic events that followed. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts look at what issues concern the voters and what change the balloting may bring. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Israel/Palestine What is happening? On 27 October, Israelis will head to the polls at a particularly fraught moment in the country’s history. The vote is the first since the deadly Hamas assault of 7 October 2023, which killed 1,318 Israelis and precipitated seismic events in Israel-Palestine and across the Middle East – not least Israel’s destruction of Gaza and killing of at least 74,000 of its people. The repercussions of this turmoil for Israeli electoral politics now wait to be seen. With Israel still entangled in several conflicts – including in the Palestinian territories, in Lebanon, in Syria and with Iran – and at the centre of increasingly passionate domestic political debates around the world, Israelis, Palestinians and millions of others will be watching closely. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the proportional threshold (3.25 per cent of the national vote) needed to enter the parliament, or Knesset, which has 120 seats. Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight, according to polls – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud Party. The other camp is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar (meaning “straight”, as in honest), a centre-right party he founded in 2025. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian Arab minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Defining party platforms is an inexact science. The vertical axis reflects domestic issues; the horizontal, external ones (including occupied territories). Box size reflects poll projections of seat numbers. Sources: israel-polls-2026.pages.dev. Party positions are Crisis Group assessments, building on Peter Lintl’s framework for Israel’s 2022 election, “Israel’s Anti-liberal Coalition”, Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, 27 January 2023 / CRISIS GROUP Notwithstanding nuances among the various parties, the 2026 contest is largely a battle between different right-wing approaches to governing an Israel that has all but consolidated its control of the Palestinian territories – ie, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. Questions that outsiders might expect to be at the centre of election debates, such as Israel’s almost 70-year occupation of these lands, preoccupy Israeli voters far less than internal issues, including the rule of law and relations between religion and state. That divergence raises complex questions about what change the world can expect to see after 27 October – and what is likely to stay the same. What are the chances of Netanyahu remaining in power? Significant, but it is too close to call. On one hand, the election comes at an especially tough time for Netanyahu. Poll numbers measuring his personal popularity and the degree of public trust he enjoys have been low for most of the period since 7 October 2023. His many years of domineering leadership – and in the view of former coalition partners, his corruption, manipulations and betrayals – have shrunk his pool of potential political allies. His Likud Party, the dominant force on the Israeli right since the 1970s, now polls lower than Eisenkot’s Yashar. Polls also show that given a choice between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, Israelis tend to favour the former general (who also garnered public sympathy after his son was killed in action in Gaza), over the sitting prime minister. For months, the parties that make up Netanyahu’s current coalition have together consistently polled well below the numbers needed for a 61-seat majority. A new hard-right party, Amcha Yisrael, led by former general Ofer Winter, could also be a handicap for Likud: it could draw votes away from Netanyahu’s party, but it could also “burn” votes, meaning render them irrelevant, since votes for smaller parties are discounted from the tally if they fail to cross the 3.25 per cent threshold. Yet Netanyahu, who turns 77 on 21 October, has long defied presumptions that his career has run its course. His skill at juggling crises is legendary; the latest ones include a lengthy trial for alleged corruption , widespread anger at his gradual overhaul of the judiciary, charges of failing to heed warnings ahead of the 2023 Hamas attack and then shirking responsibility for it, Israel’s sinking international reputation and an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, not to mention an open-ended, seven-front war spanning the Middle East. Some of his opponents, recalling what he has done in past election campaigns, worry that the pugnacious prime minister may resort to tactics aimed at dividing his opponents. In particular, they fear he may try to discourage or intimidate would-be voters among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens. Some are also apprehensive that, should he become desperate, Netanyahu might launch a new military action, perhaps against Iran, in an attempt to postpone the election . Regardless of any such manoeuvres, the far-right, religious, pro-settler coalition led by the prime minister is strong. It has survived four turbulent years in power and still enjoys a firm base of support, including among young and first-time voters. True, the Netanyahu bloc has consistently polled well below a majority needed to form a coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc – a disparate collection of right-wing, centrist and centre-left Jewish parties, as well as two lists of Palestinian Arab parties – represents a bigger proportion of the electorate in raw numbers. But several of the latter camp’s Jewish leaders have publicly sworn they would not form a government with the Arab parties, implying they might even be loath to rely on these parties’ Knesset votes to bolster a minority coalition. With neither bloc able to reach a majority alone, the Arab parties look like kingmakers. But they will not join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc is wary of inviting them into government. Source: Crisis Group estimates based on aggregate polling data up to 14 October. Some votes may be “lost” to parties that fail to reach the 3.25 per cent threshold. / CRISIS GROUP This reluctance to share power with Arabs is not new, but it has become a matter of political consensus since 7 October 2023. The Netanyahu camp’s repeated claim that its adversaries can only win by joining ranks with Arab parties is also a sign of how the far right now shapes the political climate: it appeals to anti-Arab prejudice to alarm voters and taunt opponents, as well as to trap them into possibly self-defeating commitments. The delegitimisation of any coalition that might include Arabs has increased Netanyahu’s chances of remaining as caretaker prime minister until another round of elections a few months later, not by winning, but by blocking the other side. What are the most important – and divisive – issues for Israeli voters? The elections are in part a referendum on Netanyahu, particularly on his responsibility (or lack thereof) for the 7 October 2023 events and his actions thereafter. Many Israelis blame him for a policy of accommodating Hamas’s rule in Gaza in the years leading up to the lethal attack, including the facilitation of Qatari financing; for reportedly ignoring warnings of an impending Hamas operation; for allegedly relegating Israeli hostages to the back burner among war priorities in Gaza; and for refusing to name an independent commission of inquiry into the intelligence and other failures that helped make the Hamas assault so deadly. Netanyahu’s supporters dismiss such charges as a political inquisition led by Israel’s “deep state” (which they allege includes judges and generals) along with left-leaning media and foreign-funded organisations. They defend the prime minister’s wars, arguing that he has smashed Hamas in Gaza and Hizbollah in Lebanon and (having persuaded the U.S. to join in) severely weakened the Islamic Republic of Iran, securing Israel’s uncontested regional primacy. The legacy of Netanyahu’s coalition, widely viewed as the most extreme in Israel’s history, is also at stake in that referendum. Since taking office in December 2022, the right-wing Likud and its harder-right partners have pursued an aggressive agenda of redesigning parts of the Israeli state, the occupation of the Palestinian territories and Israel’s regional surroundings. They have sought to weaken the judicial system as an institutional check (indeed the only remaining one) on the executive and legislature, at the same time as working to entrench government influence over Israeli media, tighten restrictions on civil society, extend religious laws and practices into various spheres of public life, and accelerate Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank. Meanwhile, they also stand accused of failing to support Jewish border towns affected by years of war, such as those near the Lebanese frontier, whose residents fled Hizbollah rocket fire and still consider it unsafe to return. Many Israelis who regard themselves as secular, socially liberal and advocates of mamlakhtiyut (meaning the primacy of the state over factional interests) view the government’s ambitions for extending its power as anathema. These critics accuse firebrand leaders such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir of endangering Israel’s democracy, its social cohesion and its image abroad. A fresh government unbeholden to the far right, they say, could help repair some of that damage. A dispute that encapsulates these multiple fissures concerns the conscription of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens into the Israeli army. Even as the Haredims’ share of Israel’s population grew from under 5 per cent in 1980 to nearly 15 per cent today, they continued to enjoy exemption from state service on religious grounds until 2024, when the Supreme Court overruled the exception. Two Haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which were formally part of Netanyahu’s coalition until mid-2025, sought to circumvent the ruling via new legislation that the prime minister promised to push. But they failed to reach an agreement that would pass the Knesset, as some members of the ruling coalition – including within Likud – favour universal conscription. In practice, most Haredi youths continue to dodge the draft. Opposition leaders ... dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. The Haredim are deeply unpopular with many political factions. Opposition leaders, many of whom are secular or of military background, dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. Pressure to enforce the law has mounted from exhausted army reservists whose lives have been disrupted by repeated call-ups over the last three years. The military has also repeatedly warned that it faces a personnel shortage, especially in light of the government’s demand that soldiers protect increasing numbers of settler outposts in the West Bank. For the 20 per cent of Israel’s citizenry who are Palestinian, the top issues are different. Many see blocking the far right as vital to protecting their precarious civil rights and to ensuring greater access to state resources, as well as to mitigating Israel’s worsening policies in the occupied territories. But most Arab voters also have a particularly urgent concern: restoring their personal safety amid an alarming surge in organised crime and gun violence in Arab towns, which has reached record levels under the watch of Ben-Gvir’s national security ministry and the police it oversees. The two Arab-led slates, the Joint List (made up of Hadash, which identifies as an Arab-Jewish socialist party; Ta’al, which describes itself as an Arab movement for renewal; and Balad, a Palestinian Arab nationalist party) and the Islamist Ra’am, in theory have the potential to become “kingmakers”. Neither the pro- nor anti-Netanyahu blocs will be able to reach a parliamentary majority without Arab support, either as part of a governing coalition or as outside votes to back a given coalition. But it is unclear how and to what extent such electoral clout can translate into collective gains when even most of Israel’s mainstream opposition reject partnering with them. The Arab parties themselves are not in lockstep; while Ra’am is seeking to join a coalition with only domestic concerns in mind, the Joint List stipulated that at least some demands relating to the occupied territories, such as a diplomatic pathway to a Palestinian state, must also be addressed in order for it to provide a “safety net” (ie, serve as external support) for a minority government. Is the conflict with the Palestinians playing a role in the elections? For the ruling parties, yes; for the opposition, barely. In addition to its war on Gaza, the Netanyahu government has spent its tenure hastening Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank and extending “Jewish sovereignty” through settlements, making the prevention of a Palestinian state its flagship goal. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a portfolio in the defence ministry, in particular has spearheaded efforts to advance de jure annexation. The Likud is promoting the slogan “Yamin o’ Falastin” (Hebrew for “ The Right or Palestine ”) to suggest that any alternative government would pave the way for Palestinian statehood, notably because it would depend on support from the Arab parties. Leading coalition figures loudly applaud the devastation of Gaza, with some others still promoting the expulsion of its people and the re-establishment of Jewish settlements in the strip. Opposition Jewish figures are less coherent or vocal on the topic, but by and large they do not call the settlement enterprise’s continuation into question. Some blast the government’s support for the more extremist settler agendas; virtually none supports Palestinian statehood, at least not in the near future; and many try to ignore the Palestinian question altogether. One possible exception is Avigdor Lieberman, a former defence minister and leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu, a party that largely represents Russian immigrants, and who proposes that Jordan assume responsibility for ruling Palestinians inside a truncated portion of the territory. The centre-left Democrats, led by reserve major general and parliamentarian Yair Golan, is perhaps the only Jewish party that openly supports a two-state solution, yet it conditions a Palestinian state on a host of caveats (such as maintaining long-term Israeli security control of the entire territory) and argues that in any case the time is not right for such a state to emerge. Only the two Arab lists consistently promote Palestinian rights and self-determination, though Ra’am largely relegates these issues to secondary importance in its campaign. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians, with even Netanyahu condemning what he insists are “fringe groups”. What appears to concern Israel’s mainstream media and Jewish voters, however, is less the harm being done to Palestinians than the added burden being placed on Israel’s occupying army and the state’s resources. Many also lament the further blemishes on Israel’s international image. Next to nothing has been done to stop the attacks in practice, and official policies that more broadly immiserate West Bank Palestinians, such as economic strangulation , home demolitions and land expropriation, rarely elicit comment from the (non-Arab) opposition. In a late August interview, Eisenkot said the army had “lost its control” of the West Bank due to the Netanyahu government’s policies and its emboldening of settler vigilantes. He also criticised the push to build the controversial E1 settlement , which would split the West Bank in two, as a “mistake” that has angered Israel’s allies. In a more recent interview , he claimed that a Yashar-led government would not only curb the actions of what he has called “Jewish terrorists” but also evacuate all outposts considered illegal under Israeli law in the West Bank (under international law, all settlements on occupied territory are considered illegal). It is fair to assume that he might also freeze construction of E1. But Eisenkot has also described the two-state solution as “delusional” and stressed that “I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria” (the biblical term that many Israelis use for the West Bank). Naftali Bennett – head of the Together slate, a former prime minister and past head of the Yesha settler council – is unapologetic about his support for annexing the West Bank’s Area C (ie, the part that the 1993-1995 Oslo accords left under full Israeli administrative and security control) and his rejection of Palestinian statehood. The same is true of opposition figure Lieberman, as well as two other prominent politicians, Benny Gantz and Yoaz Hendel, who have positioned themselves as unaligned with either bloc. The competing parties may differ over whether to prop up the Palestinian Authority with financial and security cooperation and who should govern Gaza, but these are peripheral rather than central disagreements. Vis-á-vis the Palestinians, the next Israeli government will assume power on a markedly different footing from when the current one was elected four years ago. In the interval, Israel has swallowed more territory and squeezed Palestinians into smaller cantons in both Gaza and the West Bank. It has razed cities and refugee camps and emboldened a settler movement that will likely remain feverishly active regardless of who is in power. There is now near-consensus among Israeli Jews about maintaining security control throughout the occupied territories – from the proverbial river to the sea. But while the far right wants to turbo-charge the settlement enterprise and turn up the heat on the Palestinians further, many Israelis would prefer to bracket the issue, reverting to policies that can manage the conflict on their terms rather than seeking a political agreement with the Palestinians. The latter approach kept the occupation out of sight and out of mind – but also kept its end out of reach. Such shades of difference could change the level of physical and economic violence meted out to Palestinians, which is no small matter. But they would barely touch the core of the occupation itself. Have Israel’s other military campaigns in the region – in Lebanon, Syria and Iran – influenced the domestic political scene? Surprisingly little. A majority of Jewish Israelis has consistently supported Israel’s wars, with tens of thousands of soldiers and reservists continuing to serve despite widespread disillusionment with Netanyahu’s government. Even when Israelis were forced into shelters for weeks on end during the present war with Iran, public support remained high. In many ways, the seven-front war of the past three years has simply accelerated Israel’s rightward shift. Such criticism as there is tends to demand a harder, not softer approach. The centrist opposition leader Yair Lapid, whose Yesh Atid party is running alongside Bennett on the Together slate, said Israel should not have stopped at assassinating Iran’s leadership but should have bombed its oil and gas facilities during the second phase of the war, which started in late February. Bennett, for his part, has made classifying Qatar as an enemy state a central talking point. In November 2024, days before a ceasefire was brokered between Lebanon and Israel, Gantz, an ostensibly centre-right former general, called on the military to bomb Lebanese government assets. What are the most likely outcomes? Barring a dramatic development, and assuming the most credible polls are largely correct, four plausible scenarios could emerge after election day: A hung parliament. Neither bloc wins a decisive parliamentary majority or ropes enough parties into supporting a minority government. This outcome is possible, for instance, if Eisenkot or his allies refuse to bring the Arab lists into the fold or to rely on their outside support. The result would be another round of elections. In this case, Netanyahu would stay on as caretaker prime minister, with his sitting coalition continuing to hold the reins of government for several months, pending a fresh vote. Yashar edges out Likud and forms a government drawn from the opposition. This scenario would likely require Eisenkot to partner in some fashion with the two lists that represent Palestinian citizens – perhaps as external backers, instead of coalition partners – with the principal aim of keeping Netanyahu and his bloc out of power. There is precedent for this arrangement (albeit in starkly different circumstances), such as when Arab parties gave outside support to Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin from 1992 until his assassination in 1995. But shifts in public opinion, especially after the 7 October 2023 attacks, make reliance on the Joint List in particular a politically fraught proposition. Parties or politicians break ranks. Following an inconclusive result, Eisenkot or Netanyahu could convince parties or individual Knesset members in the opposing bloc to defect and form a “national unity government”. There could be several permutations along these lines. For example, commentators have suggested that the opposition consider forming a government with Likud, excluding far-right parties such as Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit. Netanyahu himself has floated this possibility. Though it got broadly negative responses, there is recent precedent, albeit with mixed results. In 2020, Netanyahu persuaded Gantz, then his biggest rival, to join a coalition, causing Gantz’s Blue and White Party to split. The government dissolved only a few months later. A bloc defies the polls and clinches a parliamentary majority. This outcome is highly unlikely. It would mean that months of polls have been egregiously wrong, given that all have said neither bloc is close to winning 61 seats. A surprise could conceivably occur if several parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, thus “burning” a large share of votes, or if turnout for certain parties far exceeds expectations. Israel’s electoral system has always been prone to twists and turns, but the 2026 election’s result is arguably less predictable than usual. Dry numbers from various sources provide hints. An independent aggregator of opinion polls over recent months suggests that the chances of either bloc achieving an outright majority are well under 10 per cent. Online betting sites , which are a rough indicator of where investors put their money, give Eisenkot and Yashar slightly greater respective odds of becoming the next prime minister and largest party in the Knesset. Still, even in that scenario Eisenkot would have to decide whether to partner with Arab parties, a question he has skirted until now. The outcome may not be all that stable. Despite a reshuffling of parties and emergence of new personalities, and though the political spectrum as a whole has shifted further rightward, Israeli voters appear to be caught in the same deadlock that has largely held since 2019 – one that led Israeli voters to go to the voting booths five times in three years until the current government took office – and held onto it for four years. The recent uptick in international pressure on Israel’s West Bank policies – notably, the UK-led settlement trade ban in September – is unlikely to fundamentally shift Israeli views in the near term, though it may affect voter turnout for one side or the other. Many Israelis are distrustful or dismissive of foreign criticism, believing that outsiders do not understand their nation’s unique circumstances, are overly fixated on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or harbour anti-Israeli or anti-Semitic views. That said, they are not oblivious to the threat of isolation. They know that Israel’s brutal Gaza war, its increasingly aggressive policies in the West Bank and the proliferation of Middle East conflicts have all come at a high reputational cost to Israel, not only harming its diplomatic standing but also affecting its citizens’ interactions with the outside world. The question is whether mounting outside pressure can constructively shift Israeli calculations on war and peace after election day – regardless of the coalition that emerges. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 16 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iranians commute past a billboard depicting slain Lebanese Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and Iran's slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran on September 27, 2026. ATTA KENARE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 16 October 2026 12 minutes How War is Reshaping Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” Three years of hostilities have transformed Tehran’s network of allies in the Middle East. The Islamic Republic is now relying more heavily on itself, while adapting its relationships with partners whose diminished military utility has not necessarily reduced its commitment to their protection. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Hamidreza Azizi Senior Analyst, Iran https://x.com/HamidRezaAz Related Tags Iran Israel/Palestine Lebanon Syria Developments since 7 October 2023, when Hamas staged its deadly attacks on southern Israel, have transformed Iran’s network of state and non-state allies in the Middle East, as well as their role in Tehran’s military planning and deterrence posture. The weakening of Hamas and Hizbollah at Israel’s hands in the last three years, the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria in December 2024 and, above all, the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran launched in February have altered the vectors of Iranian influence. Together, these events have exposed the limits of an Iranian strategy that had relied chiefly on regional partners to deter adversaries and keep any armed confrontation away from Iran itself. Instead, Tehran now places greater weight on capabilities under its direct control: missiles, drones and the ability to obstruct traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. This evolution does not mean that the “ axis of resistance ”, as Iran calls its collection of allies, has lost all relevance. Rather, it means that axis members are now assuming different functions and that Tehran is approaching them differently. Yemen’s Houthis have gained particularly significant strategic value for Iran because their ability to threaten Red Sea shipping complements Tehran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. In Iraq, major Shiite factions also remain important political partners, even as Tehran increasingly turns to smaller armed groups to conduct military operations. Overall, the result is a more fragmented network in which heightened local autonomy among Iran’s non-state partners coexists with tighter Iranian control of select cells and smaller armed organisations. Nor is a weaker “axis of resistance” necessarily synonymous with diminished Iranian commitment to its partners. Hizbollah’s lesser contribution to Iranian deterrence, for example, has not reduced Tehran’s determination to protect the Lebanese Shiite movement. To the contrary, Iran has shown itself more willing to use force in Hizbollah’s defence; it also has conditioned reaching a deal terminating its hostilities with the United States on an end to Israel’s campaign in Lebanon. In other terms, Iran still may be drawn into conflicts on its regional partners’ behalf, even as they have become less capable of shielding it from attack. From the Levant to Maritime Chokepoints Prior to October 2023, Iran’s Middle East strategy centred on the Levant . Syria under Assad’s rule was the linchpin, the only Arab state allied with Iran, which provided it with substantial benefits: a land corridor linking Iran and its Iraqi Shiite partners to Hizbollah; proximity to Israel’s borders; and a logistical hub that enabled Tehran to project its influence to the eastern Mediterranean seaboard. In June 2024, Yahya Rahim Safavi , a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who was then military adviser to Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, likened Iran’s reach through the axis to that of the ancient Persian empire under Cyrus and Xerxes. The advantages of alliance with Assad explain why, over a decade of civil war in Syria, Tehran defended his regime at significant cost. Hizbollah fighters also helped the regime a great deal, battling both its domestic opponents and ISIS. Hizbollah was useful in another important way, offering Tehran a means of threatening Israel from adjacent territory, thus ostensibly deterring it from direct strikes on Iran itself. If Assad’s Syria was a linchpin of the Islamic Republic’s Middle East strategy, the Shiite movement in Lebanon was a principal engine. [Assad’s fall] deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. This arrangement has suffered severe damage since October 2023 , when Hamas – apparently taking even Iran’s leadership by surprise – attacked Israel. The Gaza campaign that Israel launched in response dealt the axis a first blow, although Iran’s relationship with the Palestinian group has never been on par with those it has enjoyed with its other affiliates. Assad’s fall – indirectly part of the chain of events triggered by the Hamas attacks – was far more consequential. It deprived Iran of its sole Arab state partner and disrupted its supply line to Hizbollah. After Hizbollah entered the post-2023 fray, Israeli counter-attacks also inflicted substantial losses on the Lebanese movement’s leadership and military assets, while causing significant death, destruction and displacement in the country. As a result, other Lebanese factions began issuing more urgent calls on Hizbollah to disarm. The setbacks reinforced one another: rebuilding a degraded Hizbollah was a far more daunting task without the Syrian channel that had previously sustained it. These losses notwithstanding, Tehran has yet to forsake the Levant. Hizbollah still has a strong, institutionalised relationship with Iran, significant political weight in Lebanon and the capacity to regroup, at least in part. The Israeli incursions into southern Syria following the Assad regime’s demise may also have benefits for Iran. The Islamic Republic may be banking on local resistance to Israel eventually creating openings for renewed Iranian influence in Syria, though this prospect remains uncertain. For now, Iran has turned its attention to an arena closer to its borders where it retains heftier clout. On 8 June, Esmail Qaani , commander ofthe Revolutionary Guards’ overseas operations arm, the Qods Force, described an emerging “security belt” stretching from the Gulf to the Red Sea. When compared to Safavi’s formulation two years prior, the phrase captures a shift in emphasis from the Levant to the maritime routes linking the Gulf to the western Indian Ocean, a theatre in which Iran’s sway comes more directly from its own place on the map. The Islamic Republic requires neither an allied state nor a non-state partner to project power in the Strait of Hormuz; it can station missiles and drones nearby or even deep inland to threaten naval or commercial vessels in these waters. Tehran’s influence over maritime routes upon which states near and far depend for trade in oil, gas and other vital commodities is boosted by its partnership with the Houthis, who can fire at ships passing in either direction through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab. Though it no longer serves as a land bridge for arms transfers to Syria and Lebanon, Iraq nonetheless plays an important part in this changing landscape. In particular, it is a locus for coordination between the Houthis and Iraqi armed groups , as well as between the Qods Force and Iraqi groups that have conducted attacks on Gulf Arab states. A More Fragmented Network The shift in Iran’s primary focus from the Levant to the seas has gone hand in hand with organisational changes. Under its late commander Qassem Soleimani, the Qods Force was the principal coordinator of “axis of resistance” activities. Since the U.S. killed Soleimani in January 2020, the Qods Force has not played the same role. Subsequent wars and leadership losses, both within the Revolutionary Guards and among its partners, further discombobulated command structures and impaired joint military operations. As a result, Iran has had to adapt its relationships with groups whose military capabilities and domestic constraints themselves have changed. It has increasingly been compelled to work through smaller groups or selected elements of established organisations. This trend has been most evident in Iraq. As the years passed after Saddam Hussein’s ouster, older Shiite political movements acquired key government positions and economic interests, thus becoming more beholden to popular constituencies. As a result, they are now more hesitant to engage in military action that risks provoking retaliation or eroding their standing. This reluctance was apparent early in the present U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, when several major Iraqi Shiite armed groups declined to mobilise on Tehran’s behalf. Iran had to rely on smaller, less prominent ones – drawn from the self-styled Islamic Resistance in Iraq – to come to its aid. Iraqi sources speak of a network of clandestine cells established by the Revolutionary Guards and operating outside established militias’ command structures that reportedly has been responsible for attacks on Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. These nimbler, smaller groups offer Tehran several advantages. They require fewer resources, they can conceal their affiliations and they can ignore the political constraints holding back their larger counterparts. Their greater ideological cohesion also arguably makes them easier for Tehran to direct. More institutionalised Iraqi Shiite groups remain important to Tehran, notwithstanding their reticence regarding military action in Iran’s defence. But their role has shifted: they are useful principally because they help Iran preserve influence in the country as well as the political space in which smaller armed groups are free to operate. Iran’s changing relationship with Hizbollah illustrates another type of adjustment to similar pressures. Though the movement retains a substantial organisation that helps Tehran sustain influence in Lebanon, Hizbollah’s military actions increasingly resemble those of a guerrilla group – quick-hitting raids that leave the group less vulnerable to Israeli airstrikes and intelligence penetration. Its use of first-person-view drones – drones using a live video feed from an onboard camera – to attack Israeli forces in southern Lebanon showcased the effectiveness of inexpensive technology, even as the movement has lost its more sophisticated capabilities. An Iranian expert with ties to both the Revolutionary Guards and Hizbollah told Crisis Group that Qods Force commanders have been directly involved in this revamping, including efforts to work through smaller units and help Hizbollah fighters adopt more agile tactics. Deterrence Moves Closer to Home, but the Axis Remains Important These changes reflect a broader reassessment of Iran’s deterrence posture. Its earlier approach heavily relied on the concept of “ forward defence ” ensured by regional partners, supplemented by the threat of direct retaliation from its own territory. The “axis of resistance” gave the Islamic Republic strategic depth , discouraging its adversaries from attacking it and keeping conflict distant from its borders. Only if that first layer of protection were to fail were Iranian missiles and drones to be used to shoot back. The past three years of war have starkly exposed the limits inherent in this arrangement. Iran’s regional network did not prevent direct attacks on the country – whether the major exchanges with Israel in 2024, the surprise Israeli attack in June 2025 or the more substantial confrontation with the U.S. and Israel beginning in February. As the deterrence value of axis partners dropped, Tehran was compelled to place greater weight on its own capabilities: missiles, drones and geographical leverage. If military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Yet, if military setbacks have transformed the role played by the axis, they have not eliminated its utility to Iran. Though the axis as a whole no longer serves as the primary foundation of Iran’s deterrence, decision-makers in Tehran believe that certain partners can play important roles in particular circumstances as they magnify Iran’s own capabilities and geographical leverage. Their experience during the present conflict with the U.S. has only bolstered this conviction. The Houthis have attained particular importance in the Islamic Republic’s thinking, which helps explain reports that Tehran has provided them with both guidance and military assistance. Tehran’s efforts in July to establish direct flights to Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen illustrated the multidimensional nature of this support: the flights both challenged restrictions imposed by Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia on Houthi rule and reportedly carried Revolutionary Guards commanders, military advisers and missile- and drone-related equipment. Hizbollah, too, has retained its usefulness for Tehran. The movement attacked Israel following February’s U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, forcing Israel to contend with an additional front and placing further demands on its air defences. True, that supporting role was a far cry from the crucial deterrent function the movement was intended to play, a reflection of its diminished capabilities. Iranian officials have nevertheless continued to frame their confrontation with the U.S. and Israel as extending to Iran’s Middle East partners, Hizbollah in particular. In June, in a remarkable role reversal, Iran launched missiles at Israel in response to its campaign against Hizbollah, thereby marshalling its own forces in defence of its partner rather than the other way around. Moreover, it conditioned its acceptance of the (short-lived) 17 June memorandum of understanding halting hostilities with the U.S. on cessation of Israeli attacks in Lebanon: the opening clause explicitly included Lebanon in the ceasefire and affirmed Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel persisted with its offensive, however, including at Ali al-Taher , a strategic Hizbollah position in southern Lebanon where Israel besieged (and, in mid-September, demolished) an underground command and weapons complex. To Iranian officials, who had reportedly sent warnings that any such act would provoke a “forceful” response, the demolition was a reminder that Iranian threats of renewed missile attacks were an insufficient deterrent. Still, Iran’s stance showcased its commitment to axis members whose military utility has faded but not been erased. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. Decades of institutional ties, ideological affinity and investment help explain Iran’s approach. According to Iranian experts interviewed by Crisis Group, several members of the security establishment regard Hizbollah’s survival in particular as being closely tied to Iran’s own security, giving the relationship a significance that extends beyond the movement’s immediate military capabilities. This outlook has surfaced in public debates. In a January 2025 interview published by Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, former diplomat Hadi Seyyed Afghahi argued that pressure on militant groups in Iraq, Lebanon and Yemen was aimed at “Iran and, more generally, the Shiites of the region”. Therefore, Tehran could not remain indifferent to these groups’ fate. Likewise, in December 2025, Ali Samadzadeh , an analyst with close ties to the regime, argued that Iran should be prepared to intervene militarily if Israel attacked Hizbollah, describing an assault on Lebanon as a prelude to renewed war with Iran. Defending regional partners, in this view, is part and parcel of protecting Iran itself. In short, where Tehran regards a partner as key to its own security, the fact that the partner has been weakened arguably – and perhaps paradoxically – provides Iran with added reason to intervene on its behalf. Efforts to curb Iranian influence by targeting allied groups may therefore draw Tehran into conflicts – a marked departure from the role these groups once played in shielding the Islamic Republic from direct involvement in hostilities. The extent of Iranian involvement is likely to depend on the particular relationship in question and the risks and costs inherent in intervention. But the bottom line is that its partners’ diminished military capabilities will not necessarily reduce Iran’s exposure to, or participation in, their respective conflicts. A Shifting Picture After three years of hostilities involving Iran’s partners and, since February, Iran itself, the “axis of resistance” is neither down nor out, but it is not what it once was, either in the function it serves or in Tehran’s relationship to its various members. The changes have been manifold. First, some of its members’ military capabilities have been significantly degraded. Secondly, direct confrontation with the U.S. and Israel has revealed the groups’ limited deterrent value and their inability to keep conflict away from Iranian territory. Finally, and partly as a result of their lessened status, they have come under growing domestic political, economic and security pressure, hindering their ability to directly participate in confrontations involving the Islamic Republic. These changes do not rule out these groups’ continued close operational ties to Tehran; nor do they mean an end to Iran’s commitment to their protection. But, together, they constrain the groups’ freedom of action. As a result, the focus of the Islamic Republic’s strategic doctrine has pivoted from allied non-state actors toward its own capabilities. This adjustment undoubtedly has preserved Iran’s ability to project power in its neighbourhood. But it does not come without serious risk, insofar as it has led Tehran to more directly bear the costs and dangers of confrontation. The Islamic Republic may well find ways to manage the consequences of its partners’ weakened clout by coming to their aid when they are endangered, giving them breathing space to regroup and using its own military assets to deter its foes, including by ensuring that others – notably Gulf Arab states – suffer the consequences of Middle East war. In so doing, Iran hopes to discourage future attacks. But this approach also risks deepening hostility among its neighbours, potentially encouraging closer security cooperation among Iran’s adversaries and heightening the very pressures Tehran seeks to reduce.
